questions.question: Distinguish between population distribution and population density, and explain why two areas can share an identical density while looking completely different.
questions.expected_answer: Population distribution is the pattern of where people are spread across an area, described in words such as even, uneven, clustered, linear, dispersed, dense or sparse. Population density is a number — the average people per square kilometre — obtained by dividing total population by total area, and it measures crowding rather than pattern. Two districts of 1 000 square kilometres each holding 50 000 people both have a density of 50 people per square kilometre, but if the first has people spread evenly across its farms while the second has all 50 000 in a single town with the remaining 950 square kilometres empty, the distributions are entirely different. Density answers 'how many'; distribution answers 'where'. This is why density is an average that can conceal everything inside it: South Africa's national figure of roughly 50 people per square kilometre describes no actual place, being the average of the empty Karoo and crowded urban townships.

questions.question: Discuss the physical factors that influence population distribution, giving for each an example of where it attracts people and where it repels them.
questions.expected_answer: RELIEF: flat or gently undulating land is easy to farm, build on and cross, so it attracts settlement, while steep rugged mountains such as the high Drakensberg repel it because of thin soils, difficult access and costly construction. CLIMATE is the strongest control: moderate temperatures with reliable rainfall support the world's great population clusters, while hot deserts such as the Sahara and Kalahari repel through drought, polar and tundra regions through cold and a frozen growing season, and equatorial rainforests through leached soils, dense vegetation and disease. WATER SUPPLY is non-negotiable: settlement follows rivers, springs and reliable groundwater, which is why the Nile, Ganges and Chinese river valleys carry ancient dense populations and why dry-country settlement is often linear along a watercourse. SOILS: deep alluvial and weathered volcanic soils support intensive farming and dense rural populations, while thin, sandy or saline soils support few. NATURAL RESOURCES attract people to otherwise unattractive sites, because minerals cannot be moved to the people. VEGETATION AND DISEASE: very dense forest hinders settlement, and vectors such as the tsetse fly have kept people and cattle out of large parts of tropical Africa. ACCESSIBILITY: natural harbours, navigable rivers and low mountain passes concentrate trade and therefore people.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's population distribution and account for it, referring to both physical and human factors.
questions.expected_answer: The distribution is strikingly uneven. Physically, there is a broad divide between a wetter, more densely settled east and a drier, emptier west, roughly along the line where average annual rainfall falls below about 500 millimetres, so the Karoo, Northern Cape, Kalahari and Namaqualand are sparsely settled, with scattered farms and clusters at water points and mining towns. Four major urban concentrations dominate. Gauteng is the largest and is an anomaly: it has no coast, no navigable river and ordinary highveld grassland, but the discovery of the Witwatersrand gold reef in the 1880s drew labour and capital, industry followed the labour, services followed the industry, and today under two per cent of the country's land holds about a quarter of its people — and the cluster persists even though the gold is largely worked out, because established people, roads and jobs hold each other in place. The Durban corridor grew around the country's busiest port and its associated industry, Cape Town from the oldest port and now from services, tourism and administration, and the Gqeberha–East London area from harbours and manufacturing, especially motor assembly. Finally, unusually high RURAL densities occur in parts of the Eastern Cape, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and the eastern seaboard, on land whose agricultural potential does not justify them. These are the former homelands such as Transkei and Ciskei, where apartheid policy confined the majority population to a small share of the land with the poorest resources — a political inheritance rather than a physical one, and the source of continuing migration to the cities.
